description: Solo builder from Mymensingh, Bangladesh. Building a simple tool that turns NASA satellite data into easy farm advice for farmers.
summary: PolarClock is a web tool that helps mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates quickly. A heat map of eight sites against twelve landing dates shows how much of the time the Sun is above the horizon (power) and Earth is in view (direct-to-Earth communication). When a launch slips, a "what do I do?" tool shows how the delay changes the chosen site and ranks the best alternatives. Timelines, a sky view from the surface, a south-pole map and a 3D/4D Moon view show how the Sun and Earth move over time. Positions are computed in the browser and were checked against real JPL Horizons output (differences under 0.04°). Terrain is not built in yet: a horizon slider stands in, and users can import horizon profiles.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: PolarClock compares eight south-pole sites across twelve landing dates. Cell colour shows the share of time the Sun is up; the blue bar shows the share of time Earth is in view. Users set mission length, minimum sunlight, minimum Earth view and local horizon height. A "launch slips" tool ranks alternatives on the new date. Each cell has a timeline (peak Sun elevation, longest dark spell, longest Sun and Earth windows, time to sunset or sunrise at touchdown), plus a sky view with play, a south-pole map and a 3D/4D Moon view. Optional: lander power and battery model, relay-satellite orbit, custom sites, terrain (horizon profile) import, an "Explain it simply" mode and CSV export.

HOW IT WORKS: Everything runs in the browser. Sun and Earth positions come from a standard ephemeris series (Meeus) with libration and lunar-surface parallax; visibility is sampled hourly against the local horizon. We checked results against real JPL Horizons output (DE441) at three sites: elevation within 0.04 degrees and azimuth within 0.17 degrees. A live comparison for lon 130E, lat -88.9, 1-8 Dec 2026 is shown inside the app. There, Horizons puts Earth below the horizon all week, so there is no direct-to-Earth link: the kind of result the tool surfaces quickly.

IMPACT: Faster, clearer scenario comparison when schedules slip. Also an educational tool for why the Moon's south pole is hard.

TOOLS: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, three.js, GitHub Pages. NASA resources: JPL Horizons (verification), LROC Quickmap (reference image and link-out), Moon Trek (link-out).

LIMITATIONS: Terrain is not built in (a horizon slider stands in; LOLA integration is future work). Power and relay models are simplified. Not for flight use.

AI USE: The code and text were created with Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant). The Horizons verification data was run and supplied by the team.
